title: Kim Kardashian's Skims offers refunds for $148 advent calendar after backlash
description: Kim Kardashian's Skims is offering customers refunds for its $148 (£110) advent calendar which has been widely criticised on social media.The accessor
body: Kim Kardashian's Skims is offering customers refunds for its $148 (£110) advent calendar which has been widely criticised on social media.The accessories advent calendar promised "twelve days of fun surprises" but has been mocked online for the quality of its contents, such as hair clips and keychains, with some comparing them to something you would find down the back of a sofa.A spokesperson for Skims has told a number of media outlets "for some, the calendar didn't meet expectations" and the company has "personally contacted every customer" to offer a full refund or credit to put towards other products". The BBC has contacted Skims for comment.The shapewear and clothing business was co-founded by Kardashian in 2019 and has made the reality TV star a billionaire, according to Forbes magazine. Skims was valued at $5bn in 2025 when it raised millions of dollars in new funding.One account on TikTok called spicychathouse compared the contents of the calendar to things "my cat collects from around my house". Another account said it looked like "a bunch of stuff that Kim Kardashian was emptying out of her bedside table".A number of accounts showed people cleaning out their own sofas and claiming they had accidentally created the Skims advent calendar.

schema.headline: Kim Kardashian's Skims offers refunds for $148 advent calendar after backlash

title: Who is David Walliams? His career and controversies including Little Britain and BGT
description: David Walliams has been accused of grooming young fans and harassing women in the workplace, after failing to stop the Guardian and ITN publishing cla
body: David Walliams has been accused of grooming young fans and harassing women in the workplace, after failing to stop the Guardian and ITN publishing claims against him.A three-year investigation, external by the two news organisations alleged the Little Britain star and former Britain's Got Talent judge preyed on teenage girls as young as 15 and young women, external for sexual purposes.He had sought a High Court injunction to prevent publication, with his lawyers arguing if allegations were made public Walliams would likely kill himself. The court refused the request.Walliams has denied all of the allegations but in a letter to journalists working on the investigation acknowledged "at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with".He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."The 55-year-old became a household name in the early 2000s through Little Britain, his comedy sketch show with Matt Lucas broadcast on the BBC.Walliams published his first children's book, The Boy in the Dress, in 2008, and his stories soon became best-sellers and led to comparisons with Roald Dahl.His 23 children's books have sold more than 50 million copies worldwide, but he was dropped by publisher HarperCollins in 2025 after allegations of inappropriate behaviour, which he denied.In 2012, Walliams became a judge on Britain's Got Talent, and was voted best TV judge at the National TV Awards (NTAs) four times. He was replaced as a judge in 2022.Before entering showbusiness, Walliams was born David Williams but changed his surname's spelling to avoid having the same name as another member of entertainment union Equity.He was married to Dutch model Lara Stone from 2010 to 2015 and they have a son.That hasn't stopped speculation about Walliams' sexuality. He has described himself as "bi-curious" and called his 2012 autobiography Camp David – but said he isn't attracted to men in the way he is to women.Not all the criticisms of Walliams have involved new standards being applied to older work.Walliams had to apologise after two charity performances, during which he yanked down not only the trousers but also the underwear of actor Jeremy Edwards and music producer Mark Ronson.In 2020, he was booed while hosting the NTAs after making a joke about Caroline Flack being out of work, at a time when she had stepped down from hosting Love Island and was waiting to appear in court, having been charged for actual bodily harm following a row with her boyfriend.Later in 2022, he was replaced as a judge on Britain's Got Talent after a Guardian story about a leaked recording of Walliams making insulting remarks about contestants during breaks from filming.In the incident, which happened in 2020, he spoke about a pensioner to whom he had taken a strong dislike and a woman who he described as "the slightly boring girl you would meet in the pub" who "you would want to have sex with, but then decide not to". He used much stronger language when talking about both.Walliams apologised, explaining: "These were private conversations and - like most conversations with friends - were never intended to be shared. Nevertheless, I am sorry."He sued the show's producers Freemantle for misuse of his private information and breaching data protection laws. An "amicable resolution" was reached, with the production company apologising for the recording being made public.Further controversy came in June 2025, when it emerged that Walliams had given two Nazi salutes during the recording of BBC One's Would I Lie to You? Christmas special.Banijay UK, which owned the show's production company Zeppotron, apologised, adding: "It was immediately acknowledged during the recording that this segment would not be broadcast under any circumstances." Walliams has never commented on the incident.Then in December 2025, HarperCollins, the publisher of his hugely successful children's books, announced that following a change of CEO, the company would no longer look after new releases by Walliams.He was dropped over allegations he had harassed female members of staff, with HarperCollins explaining that the company took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously and has processes in place for reporting and investigating concerns".The Daily Telegraph reported that an internal investigation had been opened the previous year after a complaint was made by a junior member of staff about his behaviour. This reportedly found that staff had been told to only meet Walliams in pairs and advised against going to his house.Walliams' spokesperson responded by saying he "strongly denies that he has behaved inappropriately" and that he had "never been informed of any allegations raised against him" by the publisher.Then in September 2026, HarperCollins doubled down by announcing that they were cutting all ties with Walliams and would no longer represent his back catalogue, meaning that when his books sold out in shops, they would not be replaced.

schema.headline: Who is David Walliams? His career and controversies including Little Britain and BGT

title: Tinned food and bottled water sales jump after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
description: Sales of essential goods such as bottled water and canned food soared in the 10 days following the launch of the government's "Be Ready" emergency pre
body: Sales of essential goods such as bottled water and canned food soared in the 10 days following the launch of the government's "Be Ready" emergency preparedness campaign on 22 October, research indicates.Hand sanitiser sales were up 83%, sales of bottled water rose 67% and tinned and jarred goods climbed 37%, according to data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator.The government's public awareness campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.However, Worldpanel said that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.After the campaign launch, the equivalent of an extra 400,000 people per day bought tinned meat, Worldpanel said, although the typical amount remained at 500g, which suggests a gradual stocking-up."Shoppers clearly took notice of the 'Be Ready' campaign, but this wasn't panic buying, with less than a third of households buying bottled water in October," said Fraser McKevitt, head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel by Numerator."Growth came from more people adding the recommended items on the government's checklist to their weekly shop, not from shoppers piling their trolleys high, which is very much in line with what the government wanted households to do," he said.Sales of tinned and jarred goods rose from £58.2m in the 10 days to 2 November 2025 to £79.5m over the same period in 2026.Bottled water sales jumped from £13.6m to £22.8m compared with a year earlier and hand sanitiser sales climbed from £497,000 to £908,000.Further evidence of stockpiling came from food firm Princes on Tuesday, which said demand for tinned tuna, meat and vegetables had risen following the government's campaign.Princes interim chief executive Giuseppe Mastrolia said the jump in demand "further reinforces the relevance of our core categories in providing affordable, nutritious and convenient food solutions".The "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need - for example, bottled water, and long-life food that doesn't need to be kept in the fridge such as dried fruit and nuts.Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments".Disaster recovery expert Lucy Easthope previously told the BBC that the UK was playing "massive catch up" to other European nations in terms of preparedness.These include France, Germany Denmark, Sweden, and Norway.A number of experts have been calling for the UK to put more emphasis on food security, with some arguing that the government itself should take responsibility for food stockpiling, rather than individual households.In October, a group of more than 180 experts signed an open letter, external to Burnham and first secretary of state Louise Haigh calling for local authorities to have a duty to prevent and respond to food supply emergencies.They pointed out that a government survey found that 29% of people in the UK could not afford to keep a few days worth of food in the house.

schema.headline: Tinned food and bottled water sales jump after 'Be Ready' campaign launch

title: US military aircraft leave second UK base
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Military personnel are shown loading a US Air Force plane at RAF Mildenhall on Tuesday afternoonByHarriet Whitehe
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Military personnel are shown loading a US Air Force plane at RAF Mildenhall on Tuesday afternoonByHarriet Whitehead and Frank GardnerSecurity correspondentUpdated 40 minutes agoAt least 10 US Air Force refuelling aircraft left a second airbase in Britain on Monday.Flight tracking data reviewed by BBC Verify shows the aircraft left RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk and landed at other American bases in Europe and also at Prestwick Airport in Ayrshire, Scotland.The Wall Street Journal reported that this was in response to a threat from Iran but the BBC has not independently verified that claim.Monday's departures come weeks after the US withdrew its bombers from RAF Fairford airbase over a suspected Iran-linked security incident.Image caption, US military aircraft were pictured at Prestwick Airport, near GlasgowAsked about Monday's flights, a Ministry of Defence (MoD) spokesperson told the BBC: "We do not routinely comment on the activity of other nations. Aircraft and other assets move regularly ​according to operational ​requirements."Using public tracking site Flightradar24 BBC Verify has been able to see USAF KC-135 Stratotanker refuelling aircraft leaving Mildenhall throughout Monday.Two aircraft that left initially flew to US bases in Germany and Italy. The first KC-135 then returned to Mildenhall before heading east and landing at Spangdahlem airbase in Germany. The other aircraft - having flown circuits over Aviano airbase in Italy - flew on to and landed at Spangdahlem.Flight-tracking data also shows eight other US KC-135s left Mildenhall later on Monday.An aircraft that landed at Prestwick, Scotland, on Monday is with the Nebraska Air National Guard, meaning it may have been on a regular stop before heading back to its American base.Downing Street has insisted that UK airbases are safe following this decision by the US to move some military aircraft to locations in Europe.The prime minister's official spokesperson said "the protection of our bases, both in the UK and across the world, is a top priority, we work closely with the police and our allies to protect our sites".About 3,000 military personnel are stationed at RAF Mildenhall, which is around 80 miles (130km) north of London.The BBC has found there is currently very little aircraft movement at the base, and there appears to be no additional security in place around it. The spaces from which the public can photograph aircraft remain open.The base is mostly used for refuelling and maintenance operations. Flights carrying US presidents, including Donald Trump, have often used it, and Trump transited through RAF Mildenhall on his way back to the US from the Nato summit in Ankara in July.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, US President Donald Trump walks across the tarmac at RAF Mildenhall in JulyIt has also been used as a staging area for aircraft and material bound for the Middle East. Air refuelling tankers were "forward deployed" to the region during operations against Iran.Asked about the US evacuating aircraft from RAF Mildenhall, Education Secretary Lucy Powell told BBC Breakfast she could not comment on ongoing operational matters.She added that "we take the security and safety of our bases incredibly seriously" and "we will always act on security intelligence when we need to".A US Air Force spokesperson said its aircraft "rotate between installations and operating locations for a variety of reasons including training and real world requirements". "US military aircraft are hosted in accordance with access, basing, and overflight agreements with our allies and partners. Due to operations security, we will not provide further information on movement of assets," the spokesperson added.Former UK national security adviser Lord Ricketts told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "We are talking about an airbase which houses these large tanker aircraft. Of course, they are large targets, an airbase has a long perimeter, so they are inevitably vulnerable."He added: "Nobody knows at this stage what this information was. I suspect part of it is an abundance of caution."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Aircraft left RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk and landed at other American bases in Europe and also at Prestwick Airport in AyrshireSpeaking before reports emerged of the flights leaving RAF Mildenhall, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio was asked on Monday about Iranian threats against American diplomats overseas."We've addressed it by moving people away from the threat," he said, adding: "Obviously, we're always worried about the safety and security of our personnel and their families overseas. And so, when we see anything that could pose a potential threat beyond a certain threshold, we're going to address it."Monday's departures from Mildenhall follows a security incident at RAF Fairford, a US-operated airbase in Gloucestershire.A major incident was declared after three suspicious vans were seen near that base in September. It later emerged that the US had pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.Days after the incident, Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC there were "strong indications" Iran had played a part in the incident, which Iran has denied.Two British nationals appeared in court in October in connection with an alleged Iran-linked plot. Several men have been arrested as part of the counter-terror police investigation.Iran has previously said that it considered UK bases used by the US for military strikes to be "legitimate targets".

schema.headline: US military aircraft leave second UK base

title: Faisal Islam: What the boss of US tech giant Nvidia told me about China and national security
description: Jensen Huang has the air of the late Steve Jobs about him. I have interviewed both, and the up-close charisma - and occasionally scratchy genius - is
body: Jensen Huang has the air of the late Steve Jobs about him. I have interviewed both, and the up-close charisma - and occasionally scratchy genius - is shared. Both sported a signature item of black clothing, although Huang opts for a leather jacket rather than the Apple founder's turtle neck.Both are innovators revered in the tech world.  However, Huang is now being investigated over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.Everything you have heard about Artificial Intelligence (AI) over the past few months - good, bad, revolutionary and catastrophic - is dependent on having the most powerful frontier AI models. In turn they depend on the most powerful microchips, and for years that has been this very company, Nvidia, led by Huang, and his technology rooted in repurposed games graphics and the manufacturing prowess of Taiwan.Names such as Gracehopper, Vera and Rubin mean almost nothing to the public, but are the names of chips powering the creation of AI models transforming the world.I met Huang as he held court with reporters and offered words of encouragement for the UK's tech future during US President Donald Trump's state visit to the UK in September last year.It was also right in the middle of his attempts to get Trump to lift export bans to China of some of the highest performing AI chips, specifically the H200. An export ban on a less powerful chip had already been lifted. He was, I suggested to him, one of the few people who could walk into the White House to meet Trump, and a few days later meet President Xi Jinping in Beijing.He made no secret of his views, nor his assessment that he had persuaded Trump of his case."President Trump is very clear. He wants America to win and and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them too. And the reason for that is because it's not a zero-sum game. The advance of human society is not a zero-sum game."He is probably the only person in the world that could have spoken that sentence with the authority that he might have heard personally from both these superpower leaders. However, his view about "zero-sum game" is not backed by many in national security circles. Their view is that the race to the most advanced forms of AI is entirely zero sum, and requires the West - and the US in particular - to take critical action to hold back Chinese advancement. The country that creates the most powerful AI systems, from the most powerful chips, will win, in terms of scientific development, of cracking encryption, economic growth and cyber-weapons.He made a further argument: Far from being a national security challenge, it was, in fact, better for the US that the world "including China" became dependent on US systems, what they called the "American tech stack", with Nvidia chips at its core.Huang then went even further than that, saying that President Trump "is very clear-eyed" about the idea that "this computing technology is not a national security concern". He told me "any military is smart enough to build their military on top of their own indigenous technology, and not rely on an adversary to build their technology, build their military capability".What does this show us? At that time, which is the same moment now being independently investigated over national security concerns and alleged Chinese espionage, Huang was making clear public arguments to lift export bans, and seemed to have a clear idea of President Trump's views. More than that, he was also disputing the idea that his technology, in China's hands, was any type of national security concern.Nvidia is the absolute epicentre of the AI tech boom in the US and of the global race for AI supremacy. Even if the boom turned to bust, Nvidia is still expected to remain in rude health. It has actual hard revenues of about $400bn this year. Monday's drop of about 4% of its value reflects new and extraordinary risks at this junction of tech and global politics, but the chipmaker is still worth more than $4 trillion.

schema.headline: Faisal Islam: What the boss of US tech giant Nvidia told me about China and national security

title: Phones to be banned from pupils' bags or pockets under new rules
description: Pupils will not be allowed access to their phones at all during the school day under stricter government guidance in England.Statutory guidance came i
body: Pupils will not be allowed access to their phones at all during the school day under stricter government guidance in England.Statutory guidance came into force in June, making schools and trusts legally responsible for being phone-free throughout the day.Ministers now say changes to that guidance will go beyond the current "no see, no hear" policies in place in some schools - where phones can remain in pupils' bags if they are not seen or heard - when it comes into force from September 2027.But head teachers' unions said schools would struggle to implement stricter new policies without additional funding from government.Education Secretary Lucy Powell said the government's "clear message" to parents and pupils was that "school is for learning and friendship, not scrolling".Access to phones "risks pulling children away from their learning and from each other", the government said.Schools will be able to decide how to follow the guidance. Some schools have invested in sealed pouches or secure lockers. Others collect phones at the start of the day, or have prohibited them from sites altogether.Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Powell said such policies could achieve a "whole-school culture change" - and that was "what we want to see happening everywhere".Karl Harrison, head teacher at Burnage Academy for Boys in Manchester, told the programme the school had spent £20,000 to bring in a system of metal detectors and phone pouches to prevent pupils from accessing their phones.While some felt their freedom had gone, locking phones away had increased how much pupils socialised at school, he said."People now can talk to each other, instead of scrolling on a device," he said."It's also increased levels of focus in lessons because now there's less distraction, and people are achieving higher grades."Paul Whiteman, general secretary of the NAHT school leaders union, said phones could raise "safety issues" and be an "unhelpful distraction" during the school day. But he said the more robust measures recommended under the new guidance would "come at a cost".Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said the latest guidance "does at least provide some clarity", but added that school leaders "cannot simply make mobile phones disappear"."If all schools are going to be expected to have lockable pouches or other secure storage facilities for every pupil, the cost involved will be very significant indeed," he said."This is not feasible unless the government puts in the funding required to meet these costs."Responding to questions about funding, Powell told BBC Breakfast that she wanted heads to have the autonomy to implement the policies that work best for their schools.Dame Rachel de Souza, Children's Commissioner for England, said she welcomed strong action to stop phones distracting pupils and disrupting the school day.Charlotte Ashton, co-founder of campaign group of Generation Focus, similarly welcomed the changes, saying "no see, no hear" policies were not working and pupils were still "TikToking in the toilets"."Ultimately, we need to get to a point where it's not normal for every single child to have a personal internet-enabled device in their pockets with them 24/7," she said.Shadow Education Secretary Laura Trott said she was "delighted that Labour have finally listened to us and agreed to properly ban smartphones in schools".She said it was also the "right thing to do" to have a review of safety standards around the technology used in schools, which the government has also announced on the back of calls for improved guidance.But she criticised what she called a lack of "joined up thinking" over what new tech was being allowed in classrooms.Because education is devolved, the approach to phones in schools varies across the UK.In Scotland, external, the government has said it will introduce a new law to restrict the personal use of phones in schools, and launched a consultation on the issue over the summer.In Wales, external, the Senedd recently voted against a motion to introduce a national statutory ban on phones in classrooms. The Welsh government launched a 12-week consultation in September, which it says will shape its guidance to support schools in developing a mobile phone policy.Schools are still encouraged to restrict the use of phones during the school day, but heads have flexibility over how to implement their own rules.And in Northern Ireland, Education Minister Paul Givan launched a 12-week consultation in August on whether to ban mobile phones from schools by law, calling for "a stronger and more consistent approach across our education system".Rules around phones in schools are separate from the UK's upcoming ban on social media for under-16s, due to be introduced in March.Children will be barred from accessing platforms like Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok. Vinted and eBay could also be included in the list of platforms set to be banned, the culture secretary has said.Additional reporting by Beth Rose and Nathan Standley

schema.headline: Phones to be banned from pupils' bags or pockets under new rules

title: Football Manager 27 introduces wheelchair option for first time
description: In a 2023 survey, external of gamers with disabilities by charity Scope, respondents said their top priorities included more accurate and more frequen
body: In a 2023 survey, external of gamers with disabilities by charity Scope, respondents said their top priorities included more accurate and more frequent representation in games.Will Rees, a gamer and powerchair football player for Wrexham, says it's "amazing" to see the new feature in Football Manager."I probably might play it more even though I'm not good at it," says, Will, 16."More wheelchair users will feel more included."Notable video game characters with disabilities include Hailey Cooper, Miles Morales' love interest in the Spider-Man games, who is deaf and communicates using American Sign Language. In Grand Theft Auto 5, heist mastermind Lester uses a walking stick and a wheelchair.Will, who has kyphosis (curvature of the spine) and other conditions affecting his joints, says he can see where it would be difficult for certain video games to include disabled representation.But he hopes it becomes more standard in future."We just want to be like everyone else. We don't want to be someone else or be treated differently," he says.Sports Interactive's head of production Stu Boyd says introducing wheelchairs is "step two" in the company's representation plan after it added hearing aids and eye patches in 2025."We can't do everything in one year," he says. "So we just have to keep doing it every year to try and get to that gold standard in the future."Where representation is concerned, Boyd says, "it's really important that it suits the game".Character artist Steve Norgate says the work to add wheelchair users "took a little while" because it's important to "do everything 100% right".The Football Manager team also changed elements of the in-game world to reflect the needs of wheelchair users, such as adding ramps to trophy plinths.Accessibility website Can I Play That?, external said it was a "a lovely example of going beyond just representation, and thinking about inclusion as well".It also noted accessibility improvements to the game, such as reducing the number of clicks required to navigate its menus, and the ability to customise the way information is displayed.Producer Danny Quin says they also had to change things such as camera angles and how the manager acts on the side of the pitch when matches play out."Now we've done that," he says, "we are in a place to be able to do a lot more".Boyd says it comes down to striking a balance between the team's finite resources and the features they'd like to add, but that the positive reaction online will "feed the team and feed our decisions going forwards".While there was big praise for Football Manager's latest inclusion, the announcement of the new feature did attract some negative comments online."Once that representation becomes normal and more people do it, then we might not see as much reaction to it," says Boyd. "Hopefully that'll be a more positive landscape for the gaming industry."Worthing FC owner George Dowell MBE, who has a spinal cord injury, says "silly comments" are often to be expected."Hopefully changes like this will bring more people in wheelchairs into football," he says. "Nothing will ever change if you don't change anything"."If you can see yourself you might think: 'Okay I'm really loving managing this. I want to go and try this in real life'."I know in the last few years, [developers] have been working hard to make the games more accessible for people to actually play them, which has been great. "The next step is to see ourselves fully in those games."

schema.headline: Football Manager 27 introduces wheelchair option for first time

title: 'There is no justice' - Epstein survivor on how model agency sent her to abuser's home
description: A woman raped by Jeffrey Epstein says the president of the model agency representing her put her in danger, when he sent her to two photoshoots at the
body: A woman raped by Jeffrey Epstein says the president of the model agency representing her put her in danger, when he sent her to two photoshoots at the convicted sex offender's Florida beach house.At the time, in 2009, Epstein was serving a jail sentence for sex offences against a minor but was allowed to work each day from his home."My agency's job was to protect me, and they failed. In fact, they put me in danger. And for that, they should be held accountable," she tells the BBC World Service.Roza was 18 when she was first sent to Epstein's Palm Beach home by MC2 Model Management's US branch, having only arrived in the US from Uzbekistan about a month earlier. MC2's US president at the time, Jeff Fuller, now runs another US model agency called The Source Models."My agency knew exactly where I was. So Jeff knew exactly where I was going," says Roza.She shows us an expense statement suggesting Fuller himself booked her flight home from Palm Beach, following her second shoot at Epstein's home. Fuller has previously claimed he did not know Roza was going to Epstein's house.She says the photoshoots led to her being employed as an assistant to Epstein. Other survivors have explained how the financier used the recruitment of assistants as an elaborate ruse to allow him to continue abusing young women. Roza says Epstein went on to systematically rape her.Fuller has not responded to the BBC's allegations. He has previously said he did not know Roza was being abused.We discovered through the Epstein-related documents released by the US Department of Justice [DOJ] that 10 models from MC2 met, or were in communication with, Epstein after his conviction.The files also show Epstein gave $1m (£742,000) to MC2 in 2005 - despite the agency owners telling a US publication two years later that Epstein had no involvement in their company.Testimony shared with BBC Eye also raises questions about the role played by two other individuals who were active in the model industry, and whom the DOJ files show had close relationships with Epstein - former agent Ramsey Elkholy and agency director Faith Kates.A DOJ statement from last year, that no evidence has been uncovered which would warrant further investigation against "uncharged third parties", is now being challenged by New York State senator, Zellnor Myrie.He has proposed a new sex trafficking bill to give police greater power to investigate Epstein's alleged enablers.If you are outside the UK, please watch on YouTube, externalAn email in the DOJ files, from Fuller to Epstein, makes clear the close ties between the agency and the financier. "Had it not been for you, we would have fired her months ago," Fuller writes of another model in March 2012. "And I would be careful as she blabs about things," he says.A month after Epstein's second arrest in 2019, MC2's US branch was dissolved and Fuller opened a new agency, The Source Models, which is still operating. The BBC has found that 50 models from MC2 were transferred to his new agency.We asked The Source Models to comment on our findings - it did not reply.Model agencies were useful to Epstein, says Sigrid McCawley, the lead lawyer for more than 100 of Epstein's victims."Epstein said to many people he wanted three different girls a day. Think about those numbers... The [model] scouts were really critical because they were the ones who were identifying the type of woman that Epstein liked."In the case of former agent Ramsey Elkholy, BBC Eye has discovered he tried to connect 34 women to Epstein, including an 18-year-old who was still in school.The experience of one of the women highlights how assistants would be co-opted into the structure of the abuse.Elkholy, the DOJ files show, suggested to Epstein that one of the financier's female assistants befriend this woman, before introducing her to Epstein.We spoke to this woman, and she revealed that at her first meeting with Epstein, aged 19, he sexually abused her in his New York townhouse.Ramsey Elkholy told the BBC: "I completely reject any allegation that I knew of or facilitated abuse of any kind… At the time, I had no knowledge of any abuse and I knew only his own [Epstein's] account of his 2008 [legal] case, which I misguidedly believed."He continued: "The record and published reporting show that women were often groomed by other women in his inner circle. I was never part of that circle, or indeed of any such activity… my intention was to help models find professional opportunities by introducing them to an extremely well-connected individual."If you are in the UK and you have been affected by any of the issues in this story such as sexual abuse and violence, information and support is available at BBC Action LineLawyer Sigrid McCawley says these female assistants would have had "no choice" in how they conducted themselves."These young survivors were being abused regularly. Their livelihoods were being threatened… They had to do what they were being told to do."Another model we have spoken to, Simona (not her real name), from eastern Europe, told us Epstein had raped her more than 200 times."People think that we gained something, that we agreed on this abuse in order to gain something, whether it's monetary or influential, but it's not true. We're left with deep trauma," says Simona.She says the first time she met the financier, aged 20, she was already signed with a model agency in New York, and he offered to introduce her to his "good" friend Faith Kates.At the time, Kates was the head of Next Management, one of the world's biggest model agencies. She stepped down from that senior executive position in December last year, but is still legally listed as a director of the company.Simona says at this meeting, Kates suggested she undergo plastic surgery and sent details of a surgeon to Epstein.After her meeting with Kates, Simona says Epstein convinced her to stop modelling.And just like Roza, and several other of his victims, she became his assistant. She says he went on to rape her and control every aspect of her life for nearly two years.The DOJ files show Epstein asked Kates to meet an additional five models, though it is not clear how many of these meetings took place.Lawyers for Faith Kates told the BBC: "Jeffrey Epstein was a master manipulator... Ms Kates was one of those grossly misled by Epstein. Had she known then what she - and everyone else - now knows, she would have never associated with him."They added she had never asked a model to have plastic surgery.We approached Next Management for comment, but it did not reply.Myrie told the BBC that if his bill were to become law, and "you were sending models to Epstein and you knew what Epstein was doing, or you should have known what he was doing, you will be held accountable".Roza says at the moment, "there's no justice for me, nothing's going to make everything go away".But she hopes sharing her story will encourage others to come forward."There are many, many survivors out there who never speak, because it's scary. So to all my sister survivors… you know me now. You know my name. I say, reach out."Additional reporting by Annika Grosser

schema.headline: 'There is no justice' - Epstein survivor on how model agency sent her to abuser's home

title: I took Vinted to court to get my money back
description: Mali Osmelak never imagined that selling clothes on Vinted would end with a court claim to recover almost £6,000.She started trading on the platform t
body: Mali Osmelak never imagined that selling clothes on Vinted would end with a court claim to recover almost £6,000.She started trading on the platform to earn an income while managing Crohn's disease and caring for her four-year-old daughter.But when she became a professional seller in March, she was unable to complete Vinted's verification process, leaving thousands of pounds inaccessible in her Vinted wallet. After several weeks of trying to resolve the issue, Mali took legal action. Vinted says sellers may be asked to complete verification checks to comply with legal and regulatory requirements and 98% of transactions are completed smoothly without needing help from its support team.Vinted is hugely popular in the UK with 17 million users. The online marketplace does not charge a fee to sellers for listing on there.After the BBC reported on users whose accounts had been suspended or banned, dozens of people got in touch describing difficulties accessing money held in their Vinted wallets.Mali joined Vinted in 2024 as a side-hustle. Demand for her second-hand gymwear grew rapidly and, within months, she had set up a limited company to expand the business.This year she signed up for a Vinted Pro seller account - designed for people who want to sell a high volume of items and who are registered as a business.Within weeks she had generated almost £6,000 in sales. But when she tried to withdraw the money, she discovered her account had been restricted and was told she needed to complete a verification process."I thought, 'That's OK. It's not rocket science,'" she says. "I'd set up the business with the help of an accountant and had all the information they needed."Mali says she spotted an error Vinted had made with her name and she flagged it with Vinted, but "again nothing was done and the verification kept failing". She found herself stuck in a cycle of automated responses.  In an effort to break the deadlock, she also contacted Mangopay, the payments company that at the time operated Vinted sellers' wallets and processed transactions on the platform. She was directed back to Vinted.After eight weeks without access to the money, Mali decided to take both companies to the small claims court, spending £455 in court fees.Three days after the court claim was filed, Mali says the account was "magically verified" and she could withdraw the funds.She still pressed ahead with the case though to try to recover her court fees, costs and interest. In June, she obtained a default judgement after neither Vinted nor Mangopay responded to her claim, with the court ordering the companies to pay £1,207.50.But she has yet to receive the money. She has since been informed that Vinted and Mangopay have applied to have the judgement set aside, with a hearing scheduled for December."It's been ridiculous and incredibly stressful," she says."I need that cash. I will fight it. I'm going to tell the court their system is completely broken. I needed help and nobody helped me."Vinted said: "Ms Osmelak's check was not successful because her documents did not match the name on her Vinted account. We have since helped her update it, and her account is now verified."The company did not respond to the BBC's questions about the legal action Mali has taken and continues to pursue.Mangopay said it was "bound to professional secrecy and data protection obligations. We are, therefore, not allowed to comment on individual cases involving our clients or their users, nor can we share details about specific accounts, transactions or legal matters."

schema.headline: I took Vinted to court to get my money back

title: Edinburgh Academy pupils suffered decades of 'dreadful abuse'
description: Image source, AlamyImage caption, Edinburgh Academy was officially opened in 1824 during a ceremony which included an address by writer Sir Walter Sco
body: Image source, AlamyImage caption, Edinburgh Academy was officially opened in 1824 during a ceremony which included an address by writer Sir Walter ScottByPaul O'HareBBC ScotlandUpdated 1 hour agoPupils at Edinburgh Academy suffered decades of "dreadful abuse", a report has found.Lady Smith, who chairs the Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry (SCAI), details more than 40 years of sexual, physical, and emotional abuse at the school in her latest report, external.She says the school focused on protecting its reputation and ignored complaints.Lady Smith also names four serial perpetrators of the abuse, including two who went on to offend at other schools.Edinburgh Academy, which had previously apologised for "brutal and unrestrained" historical abuse, said it was committed to facing up to "the wrongs of the past".The inquiry heard claims of historical abuse against 20 teaching staff at the private school, with most of the evidence covering the years between 1954 and 1995.Nearly 50 witnesses gave evidence, including broadcaster Nicky Campbell - who said one teacher had abused children on an "industrial scale".Figure caption, Nicky Campbell: There are a lot of people behind the scenes who made this happenPublishing her findings, former judge Lady Smith said the school had "failed to look at itself through a realistic and critical lens" for decades."It is clear it was assumed that abuse did not and would not take place," she said."When it did, the school could not accept that it had happened, failed to address it, and failed to recognise the risk of it continuing. Complacency was the order of the day."When complaints were made, they were either disbelieved or left unresolved. Staff chose not to notice and avoided intervention or investigation despite there being obvious signs of abuse."The report names two long-serving members of staff as perpetrators of abuse: Hamish Dawson, a housemaster and senior school teacher, and John Brownlee, a housemaster and deputy head of the junior school. It also singles out prep school teacher Iain Wares, who went on to abuse pupils at Fettes College and is currently awaiting extradition from South Africa; and physics teacher William Bain, who has twice been convicted of sex offences.He began his lengthy history of abuse at Edinburgh Academy before moving on to harm children in other schools.Image caption, Iain Wares is due to be extradited to the UKFormer pupil Nicky Campbell described Wares as "one of the most prolific paedophiles in British criminal history".The BBC 5 Live presenter said his overwhelming feeling about the report was sadness for the victims, including those who suffered at the hands of their fellow pupils in an atmosphere he described as "feral".The broadcaster said the effects of school abuse were "lifelong" and added: "Some of us are lucky enough to be surrounded by support and love, but it never goes away."Campbell said Edinburgh Academy was a well-run school, and that the report should not reflect on the current teachers or pupils.But he warned: "Although the 1970s might seem to be the dark ages, it's still happening in different places in different ways."We still have to be relentlessly child-centred in our approach in these matters because someone, somewhere is being abused who needs our protection." Another former pupil at the fee-paying school said the report "absolutely, perfectly captured what happened to us".Giles Moffat added: "Seeing really dangerous and evil men exposed in this instance, that is the best therapy for trauma."He said some legal proceedings were ongoing but welcomed the fact the report "cements a place in educational history for some terrible people".Laura Connor, a partner with Thompsons Solicitors Scotland, represents a number of abuse survivors from the school.She said: "Those who currently run Edinburgh Academy, while apologising for these dreadful crimes against children, have nevertheless behaved in a very difficult and uncooperative way in settling civil claims for those who were abused. That must end. "We also wait to see those remaining Academy perpetrators who have yet to be brought to justice see the inside of a Scottish court room."'Endless cycles of bullying'The report highlights the evidence of one pupil, who used the pseudonym Henry. He spent nine years at the school and said abuse was part of daily life.He told the inquiry it was normal for 11-year-olds to be groomed with jelly babies, and for them to be molested in front of other pupils."It was normal to kick, hit, and strangle, to the point of unconsciousness, 10-year-olds. It was normal to inflict physical punishment with a plank of wood with no good reason."He said grown men subjected children to "psychological belittlement" and that "endless cycles of bullying" went unnoticed or unchecked.Henry said "flagrant racism, sexism, homophobia" was ignored and there was no  safeguarding."It was normal for there to be no pastoral care, and it was normal to be somewhere where nobody, not one person, loved or genuinely cared for you," he added.Image source, Nick MailerImage caption, Lady Smith has chaired the Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry since it was set up in 2015Lady Smith said: 'None of this behaviour was "normal". Or acceptable. It was simply abusive.'"The report said as recently as 2001 the school's Court of Directors focused its reputation and how it was perceived, rather than how life actually was for its pupils.Lady Smith said Hamish Dawson's "eccentric" classroom behaviour was known about and yet "celebrated by the school". Various "instruments of correction" which he had used to abuse pupils were auctioned on his departure from the school.The report said sexual abuse extended over four decades, from the 1950s to the 1980s, and included instances of children sexually abusing other children.Physical abuse was "normalised" and children in the Prep School were regularly beaten until corporal punishment was abolished in 1988.Following the introduction of co-education in the sixth form, girls were the targets of "unpleasant and abusive misogyny". The report found there was no evidence that the school gave any consideration to the obvious risks involved.'Sombre reading'The Edinburgh Academy Survivors Group welcomed the findings and thanked Lady Smith for an "accurate and thoughtful account of the events we endured as children".The school's rector, Barry Welsh, said it had an "unwavering" commitment to facing up to "the wrongs of the past".He said the former judge's report made for "sombre reading", and "reinforces the remarkable bravery shown by our former pupils who have given evidence."We reiterate our sincere apology to all those affected by any abuse that occurred at our school."Welsh acknowledged the school could not change the past but pledged to "shape the future". He added: "We continue to support survivors as fully as we are able whilst also educating our current pupils in a caring and supportive environment."The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry was set up in October 2015 to look at the abuse of children in care in Scotland.Lady Smith has previously produced reports on abuse carried out at a number of schools, children's homes and orphanages.The Edinburgh Academy report was based on evidence hearings which took place between November 2021 and August 2023.

schema.headline: Edinburgh Academy pupils suffered decades of 'dreadful abuse'

title: Michael Carrick: Manchester United head coach's future to be discussed at Monaco meeting
description: Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick's future will be decided at a meeting attended by owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and executives Omar Berrada and
body: Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick's future will be decided at a meeting attended by owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and executives Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox in Monaco on Wednesday.Carrick's position is under threat after the club slipped to 18th in the Premier League following a chaotic 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on Sunday.BBC Sport reported on Monday there was a growing expectation chief executive Berrada and director of football Wilcox would recommend to minority owner Ratcliffe and the Glazer family that Carrick be sacked.Berrada and Wilcox will present their recommendation, though the Glazers will also be consulted, and a decision on the manager may not be announced until Thursday.Wednesday's meeting in Monaco, which is where Ratcliffe is based, was already planned and has not been organised to strictly discuss Carrick's future. However, that will form part of the talks, which could also include whether to bolster his coaching team.If the decision to sack Carrick is made at the meeting, the club want to inform him face to face. He is said to understand that United's form has made discussions over his future inevitable.United have made their worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years, but the hierarchy still believe a top five finish is possible. BBC Sport reported in October that United had sounded out former Newcastle boss Eddie Howe and ex-Germany coach Julian Nagelsmann over replacing Carrick.Former Chelsea coach Antonio Conte is known to be keen on the role, while multiple sources have told BBC Sport that former Spurs boss Mauricio Pochettino is open to a move to Old Trafford.Pochettino signed an extension to his contract as USA coach in August. However, the deal is thought to contain clauses that would allow him to leave for specific high-profile jobs. The US have a two-legged Concacaf Nations League play-off with Haiti on 14 and 18 November.The draw with Villa was Carrick's third match in charge since the club opted to give the 45-year-old more time at Old Trafford.Results during that time - a win, a draw and a defeat - were mixed, and displayed the best and worst of Carrick's reign with United shipping goals but displaying good character to come back from two goals down on three occasions. United's board toyed with sacking Carrick after the loss to Bournemouth, but decided the Englishman - and his players - had earned the opportunity to show that they could turn the club's fortunes around.It was also felt that the two-week international break in November represented a better chance for the club to properly assess the club's start to the campaign.Unfortunately for Carrick, it makes for poor reading.With one victory in 10 Premier League matches, United have made their worst start to a top-flight campaign since the 1986-87 season.They sit 18th in the table, one point above bottom-placed Crystal Palace.Only the Eagles and Ipswich have conceded more than the 19 goals United have shipped in the Premier League this season.It is hard to believe given the club's current predicament just how quickly Carrick's tenure has soured.Looking back, the 48 hours before United's season-opening match at Hull were pivotal.With Benjamin Sesko still trying to ease his way back from the shin issue that ended his previous campaign early, Amad Diallo suffered an ankle injury that would rule him out for seven weeks. It meant Carrick was deprived of his first-choice striking alternative, with Bryan Mbeumo having to play on the right of the attack.Carrick instead turned to Matheus Cunha, whose preference for dropping deep took him into the spaces captain Bruno Fernandes likes to occupy.It neutralised United's attack on a day they seemed ill-prepared to meet the physical challenge of an opponent motivated by their long-awaited Premier League return.In his role as interviewer for Nordic broadcaster Viaplay, former Norway and Middlesbrough striker Jan Aage Fjortoft later claimed United had lacked passion - something Carrick dismissed as "ridiculous"."It's one game," Carrick told the media afterwards.The following week, United were losing to Ipswich - another newly promoted side. Only a slip from Marcelino Nunez inside his own half allowed Cunha to tee up Fernandes for an undeserved equaliser. The Portugal playmaker, who had just been crowned PFA Player of the Year for 2025-26, went on to complete a hat-trick in a 5-2 win.He has scored just once - a penalty against Villa on Sunday - in the league since.After the Ipswich win came a trip to Everton. Twice United led, the second occasion when Sesko struck two minutes from full-time after coming on as a substitute. Deep into stoppage time, Ainsley Maitland-Niles drove home from long range to deny the visitors.Asked how confident he was in his side's ability to react to a disappointing start to the season, Carrick snapped back: "It's not been that bad."What happened next, however, was.Time and again, United's fitness was called into question. They struggled badly against a Manchester City side reduced to 10 men in the first half before their rivals benefited from an Erling Haaland goal that referees' chief Howard Webb later admitted should not have stood.Carrick's complaints were justified - but they masked a poor performance from his team.After taking a 2-0 lead inside 10 minutes against Brighton in the EFL Cup, United were outplayed and beaten, thanks to two goals in four second-half minutes.The fine margins United benefited from during Carrick's interim spell were now going against them, and his coaching staff - lauded months earlier - could not find an answer.Carrick called Cunha's injury-time equaliser against a Fulham side who started the game bottom of the table a positive to build on. But immediately after the international break, United were held to another draw - conceding in injury time to an out-of-form and 10-man Tottenham.The whirlwind was starting to pick up strength.Lisandro Martinez, who scored an own goal against Fulham, was at fault for Spurs' leveller, which made his post-match outburst after the 2-0 Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid more amazing.The Argentina defender criticised United's summer recruitment and placed the blame at the door of "the technical director" - Wilcox.By the time of Martinez's outburst, Sesko and left-back Luke Shaw were injured. Marcus Rashford has not played since. The rotation at left-back that eventually led to Carrick starting five different players in that role was in full swing.After conceding in the opening minute against Atletico, Como scored inside the first two in a 4-1 Champions League defeat for United. Fernandes came out afterwards and criticised Carrick's tactics.He was dropped for the Bournemouth game, but returned as captain at Chelsea. United were beaten in both matches.With just three wins in 15 matches in all competitions this season and United stuck in 18th in the Premier League, Carrick is set to pay the price.

schema.headline: Michael Carrick: Manchester United head coach's future to be discussed at Monaco meeting

title: Tories pledge to cut benefits for children with 'milder cases' of ADHD
description: The Conservatives have pledged to save £2.8bn a year by ending Disability Living Allowance (DLA) payments to families of children with "milder cases"
body: The Conservatives have pledged to save £2.8bn a year by ending Disability Living Allowance (DLA) payments to families of children with "milder cases" of behavioural disorders, learning difficulties or ADHD.The policy is one of a series of measures which the party says will save £36bn from the welfare budget. Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said the system risked putting children on a "conveyor belt" towards a "lifetime on benefits". Labour described the Tories' plan as a "charter for homelessness and human misery that would push people into hardship and end up costing the state more".DLA for children allows parents to claim between £30.30 and £194.60 per week to help cover the additional costs that come with raising a disabled child.The child must either have difficulty getting about or need more looking after than a child of the same age who does not have a disability.The Conservatives say child DLA is the "fastest growing benefit in the UK's welfare system", citing government statistics showing the number of cases had risen from  521,476 in 2020 to 914,000.The party is proposing that in cases where a claim is for a behavioural disorder, learning difficulty or ADHD, only those with the highest need will be eligible for cash payments.Under the party's plans, those with the most severe conditions, representing around 30% of cases, would continue to receive payments.The remaining 70% would lose the money but instead receive support through mental health services and family hubs, into which the Conservatives have said they will invest £1bn. The changes would apply to new claims and reassessments. Those with physical disabilities would be exempt.The party's other previously-announced cuts include: £13.7bn from changes to sickness and disability benefits including restricting payments to claimants with "milder mental health issues and neurodiversity conditions such as anxiety, depression and ADHD"£9.5bn by making it harder for foreign nationals to claim benefits £4.5bn by reducing local housing allowance payments£3.1bn by reintroducing the two-child benefit cap£1bn from tackling fraudSetting out the party's plans, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said: "The reality is that millions of people can and do contribute to our economy, to their families, to their communities even when they face serious challenges. "Double amputees run marathons. People who are housebound do wonderful creative work from home. People with autism run some of the biggest tech companies in the world."If you tell a young person that their ADHD means they are defective and will never amount to anything, that mindset is likely to be more destructive to their future than the condition itself."The Labour government has said it wants to bring the benefits bill down but has not set out a timetable for any reductions.More details of its plans are expected to come after former minister Alan Milburn has published his review on young people not in education, employment and training. Both Milburn's review and a review into disability benefits, co-chaired by Minister Sir Stephen Timms, will be published in November. Asked about Milburn's review, Whately said he was "rolling the pitch for more welfare spending" adding: "We're in no question and no doubt that you can make savings from welfare - it's just that Labour doesn't want to do that."A Labour Party spokesperson said: "The Conservatives designed and implemented this benefit system, which has driven large numbers of people to be signed off and written off. "Labour is tackling the collapse in face-to-face assessments, bringing in personalised employment support for sick and disabled people and spreading opportunity to young people through the Youth Guarantee."The Child Poverty Action Group said: "These proposals would take the UK back to the dark ages, causing the biggest overnight increase in child poverty since records began."

schema.headline: Tories pledge to cut benefits for children with 'milder cases' of ADHD

title: Anthropic heads for lower than expected $1.3 trillion valuation in stock market debut
description: Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude chatbot, could be valued at around $1.3 trillion (£1 trillion) when it lists its shares for sale on New Yo
body: Anthropic, the AI company behind the Claude chatbot, could be valued at around $1.3 trillion (£1 trillion) when it lists its shares for sale on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.The loss-making company says it will offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each and will raise up to $64bn when it floats this month.It would value Anthropic at between $1.1tn and $1.3tn which, although large, is below the $2tn some backers of the firm predicted in summer, according to the Financial Times.It is floating at a volatile time for AI firms. After last week's US midterm elections, the Nasdaq fell sharply on concerns a Democrat-led Congress could slow development of AI and the buildout of data centres.There are also wider fears over the billions of dollars being spent on AI and whether it will pay off.In its most recent results for the six months to the end of June, Anthropic's revenues jumped to $16.2bn from $1.1bn in the same period last year. However, its pre-tax loss jumped to $80.7bn from $12.9bn.Fiona Cincotta, a senior market analyst at City Index, said the $64bn Anthropic wants to raise is "fairly bullish" within "the volatility [and] concerns towards AI that we've seen in sort of particularly last week".She told Reuters: "It's showing that they are still sort of upbeat about the outlook as far as AI is concerned and that obviously that they think that the demand is going to be there."At $1.3tn, Anthropic's possible valuation is below SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company, which listed its shares in June and was valued at nearly $1.8tn. Anthropic is just five years old. It was co-founded in 2021 by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei along with five others - all of whom worked at OpenAI, the rival AI giant behind ChatGPT.

schema.headline: Anthropic heads for lower than expected $1.3 trillion valuation in stock market debut

title: Met Police investigating more 'potential criminal allegations' about Russell Brand
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByHelena Wilkinson & Paul GlynnBBC NewsUpdated 1 hour agoThe Metropolitan Police have said several people contacted them dur
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByHelena Wilkinson & Paul GlynnBBC NewsUpdated 1 hour agoThe Metropolitan Police have said several people contacted them during the trial and following the conviction and sentencing of the disgraced comedian Russell Brand, "to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation".A Met spokesperson said: "Detectives are assessing this information as part of their ongoing enquiries."Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Det Supt Andy Furphy, who led the Brand investigation, said officers were "looking at exactly what we've got" and "whether they're information that points to behaviour or whether they could constitute a criminal offence".Brand is already being investigated over rape allegations from two more women. He has been interviewed under caution in connection to those allegations.On Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison, after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.In his sentencing remarks, judge Joel Bennathan described him as a "sexual predator" and criticised his "staggering arrogance".The 51-year-old was sentenced to nine years for rape, with an additional 18 months, nine months and eight months for three counts of sexual assault. The latter sentences are to run concurrently.He was found guilty of the charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009.The head of the Metropolitan Police, Sir Mark Rowley, said on Friday that he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations about him.The Downfall of Russell BrandHow the outspoken comedian went from Hollywood stardom to a prison sentence.Asked by BBC Breakfast how the women in the case who gave evidence in the trial were coping, Furphy said: "Some have found it deeply distressing because of the amount of media attention wrapped around it."Even Russell Brand himself before and during trial was putting material online, but we continue to support them."He noted how the conviction "could not have been achieved" without their "bravery, their courage, their resilience throughout the whole criminal justice process".He continued: "It's deeply personal and quite harrowing to be a victim of rape and sexual assault, and to have to tell anybody about it, let alone police officers."But I'm glad they did. I'm glad they put their trust in us."Image source, James Manning/Press AssociationImage caption, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy speaking to the media outside court after Brand was convictedMP Dame Caroline Dinenage has re-iterated her concerns about Brand being able to post videos online in the build-up to and during his trial to his millions of followers."This does continue to be an issue that he has made money throughout the process on his social media platform," she told the same BBC TV programme."It just felt very odd that during the height of when there was a police investigation and some really serious allegations in the paper, that he was able to go online to his two and a half million followers, denying everything and putting his side of the story forward."That was an opportunity that his victims didn't have."Image source, Elizabeth Cook/Press AssociationImage caption, Brand did not react in the dock as he was sentenced. Before being taken down to the cells, he mouthed "I love you" to his wife Laura Brand, who was in the court.In September 2023, after the Sunday Times and Channel 4 Dispatches allegations were made against Brand, Culture, Media and Sport (CMS) Committee chair Dame Caroline wrote to social media companies Rumble, X, TikTok and Meta.She asked if they would follow YouTube in cutting off Brand's income on their platforms. Rumble publicly refused, and X said it does not take action against accounts that have not broken its rules or the law. TikTok said he had never been monetised there."We know that he had used his following [online] to try and cow people into silence," added Dame Caroline."And the fact that they [the women] were able to come forward and tell their story and tell their truth and secure this conviction because of it is unbelievably impressive."

schema.headline: Met Police investigating more 'potential criminal allegations' about Russell Brand
